meta.title: Who really said "The great tragedy of Science — the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Darwin. Thomas Henry Huxley coined it in his 1870 British Association address "Biogenesis and Abiogenesis," describing Buffon and Needham.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The great tragedy of Science — the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Darwin — it's Thomas Henry Huxley, from his 1870 address "Biogenesis and Abiogenesis." The exact wording is confirmed in the primary source.

answer.label: Not Charles Darwin — actually Thomas Henry Huxley
answer.sourceLine: Huxley wrote these exact words in “Biogenesis and Abiogenesis,” his 1870 Presidential Address to the British Association, describing how Spallanzani’s experiments demolished Buffon and Needham’s theory of spontaneous generation. The wording is confirmed in the primary text; the popular attribution to Charles Darwin — Huxley’s friend and ally — is a long-running error.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Biogenesis and Abiogenesis” (Presidential Address, British Association for the Advancement of Science, Liverpool)
Nature, 15 September 1870; later in Collected Essays, Vol. VIII, p. 229

source.excerpt: But the great tragedy of Science — the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact — which is so constantly being enacted under the eyes of philosophers, was played, almost immediately, for the benefit of Buffon and Needham.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the line to Huxley’s 1870 Liverpool address, published in Nature on 15 September 1870, and documents its later misattribution to Charles Darwin ↗.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section as Huxley’s “Biogenesis and abiogenesis” (1870), Collected Essays Vol. 8, p. 229 ↗.
The exact sentence appears in the primary text of the essay, in the passage about Buffon and Needham ↗.
source.excerptNote: The “ugly fact” was Lazzaro Spallanzani’s demonstration that properly sealed and heated infusions produced no life, refuting Buffon and Needham’s hypothesis of self-generating “organic molecules.”
source.rightsNote: The address was delivered in 1870 and first published in Nature that same year; Huxley died in 1895. The work is long out of copyright and in the public domain worldwide.

author.name: Thomas Henry Huxley
author.heading: About Thomas Henry Huxley
author.bio: Thomas Henry Huxley was a self-taught English biologist who became the era’s foremost champion of evolution by natural selection, earning the nickname “Darwin’s Bulldog.” A gifted lecturer and essayist, he coined the term agnostic and did pioneering work in comparative anatomy and palaeontology. His public addresses, including the 1870 British Association speech that produced this line, made him one of Victorian science’s most quotable voices — which is partly why his words are so often reassigned to his more famous friend Darwin.

misattribution.heading: Why people credit Darwin
misattribution.intro: Huxley was Charles Darwin’s closest public defender, so lines about hypotheses and inconvenient facts drift naturally onto Darwin’s name. The reassignment is more than a century old.

items.why: Darwin never wrote this. Quote Investigator documents the misattribution to Darwin appearing in a newspaper as early as 1901 ↗; it has since spread widely online because Huxley’s evolutionary advocacy is popularly conflated with Darwin’s.
Quote Investigator also records the line being “implausibly assigned” to Benjamin Franklin (1948) and John Tyndall (1878) ↗ — neither originated it.

Later paraphrases swap “theory” for “hypothesis” and “killed” for “slaying” — e.g. Francis Galton’s 1908 “a beautiful theory, killed by a nasty, ugly little fact,” which he attributed to Herbert Spencer, who heard it from Huxley ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Thomas Henry Huxley’s, from his 1870 address “Biogenesis and Abiogenesis,” as documented in the sourced Wikiquote entry ↗ and confirmed in the primary text.

context.heading: What the line means
lead: Huxley delivered the line in the middle of a scientific debate about abiogenesis — whether living things can arise from non-living matter. He was recounting how the eighteenth-century naturalists Buffon and Needham had proposed an elegant theory of self-generating “organic molecules,” only for Lazzaro Spallanzani’s careful experiments to refute it almost at once.
The phrase has since become a favourite shorthand for the self-correcting nature of science: no matter how attractive an idea, a single well-established observation can bring it down.
